entities.name: Pericles
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pericles (c. 495–429 BCE) was an Athenian statesman, orator, and general who presided over Athens during its Golden Age—the most brilliant period of artistic, intellectual, and democratic achievement in the ancient world. Under his leadership (c. 461–429 BCE), Athens became the cultural capital of the Greek world and the birthplace of Western civilisation's defining institutions.

Pericles championed radical democracy, extending political participation to all male citizens regardless of wealth. He initiated the building programme that produced the Parthenon, the Propylaea, and the Erechtheion on the Acropolis—financed controversially from the Delian League treasury meant for collective Greek defence against Persia.

His 'Funeral Oration' of 431 BCE, recorded by Thucydides, remains the most famous articulation of democratic ideals in Western literature: 'Our constitution is called a democracy because power is in the hands not of a minority but of the whole people.'

Pericles died of the plague that devastated Athens in 429 BCE during the Peloponnesian War he had helped provoke. His death marked the end of Athens' Golden Age. As Thucydides judged: 'In name it was a democracy, but in practice it was government by the first citizen.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Pericles' radical democracy and building programme transformed Athens into a cultural capital, shaping Western civilization's defining institutions. His leadership during Athens' Golden Age had far-reaching consequences for the development of democratic governance and the arts.
